items.title: 5x faster Edge Functions: V8 isolates to Firecracker MicroVMs
items.author: jbott
items.summary: About a billion Edge Functions run on Netlify every day — Sunweb personalizing pages, Loto-Québec routing traffic on a cookie check, and hundreds of thousands
items.text:
About a billion Edge Functions run on Netlify every day — Sunweb personalizing pages, Loto-Québec routing traffic on a cookie check, and hundreds of thousands of other sites doing everything from personalization to routing to auth. All of it runs on a full JavaScript runtime that scales with our customers’ traffic.

This poses a significant technical challenge, as we strive to make the latency as low as possible. To run tens, sometimes hundreds of thousands, of edge functions per second, we need to process each request, route it correctly, allocate compute capacity, and boot both our platform code and the customer’s code. All of that has to happen within milliseconds.

Over the past several months, our team has rebuilt the infrastructure behind Edge Functions, working closely with the team at Unikraft, who wrote about the experience from their side. In the past, requests went out to a hosted execution service. Today, they run on MicroVMs inside our own edge network — roughly 5x faster at the median. That shift also improves security and reliability, and opens up more possibilities for running complex compute at the edge.

This doesn’t change how Edge Functions are written or used — URL imports, npm packages, Node built-ins, netlify.toml declarations, local development — all of it works exactly as it did before. It’s now faster and more resilient. In this article we’d like to share more about the new architecture and our learnings on building a new compute platform that’s able to serve high volume at a low performance overhead.

The numbers, first

An edge function runs in front of a site, on every request that matches it. The time it takes is time a customer spends waiting, so milliseconds here count for more than they do almost anywhere else.

A warm invocation — routing to a compute node, entering a MicroVM, running the function, producing response headers — now costs:

~5–6ms at median (p50), down from 25–40ms on our previous infrastructure

47.4% faster p99 invocations

99.998% availability

5x faster edge function log delivery

A cold invocation is worth stating too. When a request arrives in a region that no compute node has seen before, it needs to fetch the relevant images before it’s able to run anything. This happens on about 1.2% of invocations and takes about 9ms on average.

What happens during request time

What follows is the path a single request takes, in order: it arrives at the edge node, it’s turned into a specification, is routed to a compute node, and then handed off to a MicroVM that may or may not already exist based on whether it’s a cold or warm invocation.

Request arrives at the edge node

Every request lands on the Netlify edge node closest to the client. The node terminates the TLS connection and checks the request path against the Edge Functions’ routes for that deploy.

If nothing matches, the request carries on to the cache and onto the origin as usual. If a route does match, this is the point where the request used to leave our network. With our old infrastructure it went out over the internet, ran the edge function, and came back to us to pass on. With the new compute platform, the request is forwarded to a compute node within our network.

Creating an Edge Function service

When the compute node receives the request with the machine specification and the service ID, it first checks to see if a service with that ID already exists. If it does, it forwards the request into the service for it to send into the MicroVM. A service lets us have multiple MicroVMs associated with the same site’s Edge Functions, and allows us to configure parameters for when to scale MicroVMs in and out. For example, we configure each service to only allow a fixed number of requests to be handled by a MicroVM before we shut it down, to avoid MicroVMs running indefinitely. We use the same parameters to know when to eagerly boot up another MicroVM in anticipation of one shutting down.

If a service for the site’s edge functions doesn’t already exist on the compute node, one is created, and we check to see if we have all the images in the machine specification on disk. If any are missing, they’re fetched from the edge node and written to disk. This approach means we only fetch the edge function images that are receiving traffic in that region.

The edge node writes a spec

Before the request goes anywhere, the edge node writes a specification for the machine that will run a function. The spec names three images: the runtime, our platform image, and the edge function image. It also sets the CPU, memory, and connection limits.

The spec travels with the request, on every request. Its hash and site-specific information is computed to become a service ID. This allows for isolation, since two deploys with different code or different environment variables are different services, and they never share a MicroVM.

This isolation matters most for failures we don’t want to be possible. A potentially compromised deploy runs in a separate MicroVM, and even if it escapes the runtime, it cannot poison other customers or the compute layer itself. V8 isolates, no matter their name, do not provide this level of isolation.

Choosing a compute node to run an edge function

Each region has a group of compute nodes. The edge node picks one for the service using rendezvous hashing: the same service lands on the same node every time, which is what keeps a MicroVM warm and the code already on disk and in cache once it’s been read. This stickiness gives us a caching strategy. If we spread requests evenly across the swarm, we’d end up with a higher level of cold starts.

It’s important to remember that while sending every request for a function to the same compute node is the fast path, it’s also how a hot spot forms — where one busy function competes for resources with everything else on that box. A service taking a large share of a region’s traffic pinned to a single node will saturate the node at the expense of other services.

We balance this by relaxing the stickiness. Over a certain threshold, we spread the service across a slice of nodes. This lets us absorb sudden spikes in traffic from a single customer without affecting other services that hashed to the same node.

Finally, once a node is chosen, it pulls in the function’s code. A compute node that has served the function before already has it. A node seeing it for the first time fetches it once and caches it, so only the first request pays that cost.

Starting the MicroVM

Each function runs in its own Firecracker MicroVM. These are created in under a millisecond and start in about 2ms at p99, because the VM starts a stripped-down Linux environment rather than a full operating system. The edge function’s files are mounted as an uncompressed EROFS image and then memory-mapped, so the VM reads only the parts of the bundle it actually uses instead of loading all of it.

When the MicroVM boots up and the JavaScript server begins to listen on a port, we take a snapshot of the MicroVM. When the edge function isn’t being invoked, the MicroVMs running it scale to zero instead of sitting idle. The next time it’s invoked, we start a new MicroVM from that snapshot. The snapshot is memory-mapped, so the VM can start executing without waiting for the entire snapshot to be read back into memory.

The lifecycle of the VM — boot, snapshot, restore, and scale to zero — is the work of Unikraft’s product. We worked closely with them throughout the migration to make sure it holds up under our request volume and traffic patterns.

Running and response handling

After operating this project for several years, we already had learnings we incorporated to maximize performance and the ability to debug. At scale, we’ve run into all kinds of issues, from running out of ports on virtual switches to DNS (we were surprised, but it wasn’t always DNS).

In this iteration, we made sure compute nodes run local DNS resolvers. We’ve also expanded the metrics we collect, recording things like boot time, time to first port open, and time to start user code. There are also several circuit breakers in place to ensure prompt rerouting and decommissioning of compute nodes.

That’s the whole path, and on a warm instance it adds about 6ms. None of it leaves our network, and we’re in control of the whole request cycle. Everything above happens between the request arriving and the response going back out.

Designing resilient compute infrastructure

When you build a system like the one described above, you’re optimizing for two things at once: the end-user experience and rollout resiliency. We need to be able to roll out changes quickly but balance that with the ability to roll back just as quickly.

The compute nodes are built from a base image published by Unikraft and install a set of packages. These nodes are built separately from our edge nodes for a couple of reasons: it keeps our edge nodes lightweight and fast, it lets us use different instance types for our compute nodes, and it lets us scale these nodes independently.

A control plane keeps track of which compute nodes exist and which are healthy, and the edge nodes poll it for that list. It’s also what drives a deploy — a new fleet comes up alongside the running one, scales to match it, and takes over traffic only once it’s healthy.

Building the compute infrastructure has required close collaboration with the Unikraft team. Throughout the migration, we’ve worked with them on testing correctness, handling large volumes of requests, and building capabilities specific to our platform.

It’s live

The work to rebuild our edge compute architecture is more than just a speed boost. It’s a faster foundation we can keep building on and have more control over. The best part is that it’s already serving your production traffic today, at the same pricing, with no migration step and nothing to change in any project.

Running the compute ourselves means the ceiling on Edge Functions is ours to raise. Three things this makes tractable that weren’t before:

npm package support, out of beta. npm packages work in edge functions today, in beta, with caveats around native binaries and importing files at runtime. A real VM with a real filesystem removes most of the reasons those caveats exist.

Room to revisit the operation limits. The documented limits of 50ms of CPU per request, 512MB of memory, and 20MB of compressed code came from the isolate-based execution model.

Compute inside our own network. Anything that depends on controlling the network path, instead of reaching a third party across the internet, is now something we can build.

We’re not done here. The limits and rough edges we couldn’t touch before are the ones we’re working on now, so stay tuned.

Markdown notes that run shell commands, code, SQL, and AI promptsMarkdown notes that run_

New subscriptions this week

Stripe API notes

New subscriptions this week

---
profile: stripe
---

Monday check on last week's signups. The stripe profile holds the API key and database URL. Endpoints are in Stripe API notes. #growth

sh

curl -sG https://api.stripe.com/v1/subscriptions -u "$STRIPE_KEY:" \
-d limit=100 -d "created[gte]=$(date -v-7d +%s)" > subs.json
jq -r '.data[].plan.nickname' subs.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

24 Pro, 11 Team, and 3 Business since last Monday.

python

import json
subs = json.load(open("subs.json"))["data"]
mrr = sum(s["plan"]["amount"] for s in subs) / 100
print(f"{len(subs)} subscriptions, +${mrr:,.0f} MRR")

38 new subscriptions, adding $2,682 in MRR.

sql

select source, count(*) as upgrades
from accounts
where upgraded_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
group by source order by upgrades desc;

The database agrees: 38 upgrades. Newsletter 17, docs 12, referrals 9.

prompt

Write this week's growth update from this note for #team

A Markdown notebook for developers and DevOps who keep commands in their notes. Write a note, press ⌘↩ on a code block, and its output streams in beneath it. In your shell, in your project, on your machine, or on a server.

Install Ledge Server$ curl -fsSL https://ledge.sh/server.sh | shCopy

Free and open source · Apache-2.0 · macOS on Apple Silicon · Linux · Windows 11 with WSL · iPhone and iPad · Android (beta)

Each note has its own shell

Shell blocks run in a persistent shell that belongs to the note. A cd, an exported variable, or an activated virtualenv carries into the next run.

⌘↩ runs the block under the caret. Output streams in beneath it.

⇧⌘↩ sends the block to the note's terminal drawer, a second shell you can keep typing in.

A running block takes input. Answer a sudo password or a [y/N] in the output panel.

cwd: and env: in the frontmatter set where the note's shells start and what they carry.

norun on a fence takes the Run button away. Use it for a command you are quoting, not running.

Docs: Running Code

Invoice rounding bug

Totals drift by a cent on partial refunds. Repro first. #billing

sh

cd services/billing && source .venv/bin/activate

sh

pytest -q --tb=no tests/test_refunds.py

Keep your notes on a server

Point Ledge at a machine over ssh and the notes live there. The server holds the files and runs the shells. The app on your computer is the window onto it.

No account, no service, and no port to open. The only thing between you and the server is ssh.

Shells and running blocks belong to the server. Close the laptop and they keep going. The output is waiting when you open it again.

Your computer, your phone, and a second window can all be on one server at once, each with its own tabs.

Sign in with an ssh key, or with a password kept in the system keychain. Ledge pins the server's host key and refuses any other.

Install with the command below. ledge backup puts an encrypted copy of the notes in an S3-compatible bucket every hour.

Install Ledge Server$ curl -fsSL https://ledge.sh/server.sh | shCopy

Docs: Keep Notes on a Remote Server

---
cwd: ~/api
---

Cut 2.4.2 from the server, not the laptop. The build takes a minute.

The same notes on your phone

Ledge runs on iPhone and iPad as a window onto the same server. The phone holds no notes. It reads, edits, and runs what is on the server.

Read, edit, and create notes with live preview. Search, tags, backlinks, daily notes, and wikilinks all work.

Tap Run on a block and it runs on the server. Switch apps and it keeps running. The output is waiting when you come back.

^C, ^D, Escape, and the arrow keys sit above the keyboard, so you can interrupt a command, quit a pager, or move around in htop.

Scan the pairing code that ledge pair prints on the server. The phone signs in with a key made in the Secure Enclave that never leaves it, and that key can speak to Ledge and nothing else.

Locked notes unlock with the passphrase. The phone stores none of it.

Docs: Ledge on Your Phone

Media server

Two episodes transcoding. Check before starting a third.

Run blocks on other machines

Add a host: line to the frontmatter and every run in the note happens over ssh on that host. The note itself stays where it is.

Declare several hosts and Ledge asks which one on every run. Enter repeats your last pick.

Mark a block confirm and Ledge shows the code, names the machine, and asks before running it.

Authentication is your own ssh. Keys, agents, ~/.ssh/config, and 2FA work as they do in a terminal.

The note's cwd and env travel with the run. Profiles and secrets never do.

python, node, and other interpreted blocks run on the host too, with a per-machine interpreter override in Settings.

Docs: Run Code on Remote Hosts

---
cwd: ~/Projects/api
host: staging, deploy@prod
---

Stale session keys after the 2.4.1 deploy. Flush staging, verify, then prod.

sh confirm="Flush the session cache?"

Put notes side by side

⌘D splits the view left and right, ⇧⌘D top and bottom, and either side can split again. Each pane has its own tabs.

Every note keeps its own shell, so two panes are two working environments. A run keeps streaming in the pane you left.

Drag a tab to another pane. It keeps its caret, scroll position, undo history, and any output still streaming.

⌃Tab cycles tabs. ⌃1 to ⌃9 jump to one by position.

Each workspace saves its layout and restores it at the next launch. ⌘1 to ⌘9 switch workspaces, layout and all.

One terminal drawer spans the window and follows the focused note.

Docs: Panes and Tabs

cwd: ~/Projects/api

Trial length bug

Some trials end a day early.

Secrets stay out of your notes

A profile is a named file of environment variables kept outside your notes folder. A note that names it gets the variables in its shells. The note carries only the name.

profile: deploy in the frontmatter reads ~/.config/ledge/profiles/deploy.env, a plain dotenv file readable only by you.

Notes get synced, backed up, and read by agents. A profile value stays on the machine.

Any number of notes can share one profile. An env: line overrides a value for one note.

A built-in editor shows the values masked, with one toggle to reveal them.

envFile: .env loads the project's own dotenv for everything that is not a secret.

Docs: Profiles and Secrets

---
cwd: ~/Projects/api
profile: deploy
---

Backup restore drill. The AWS keys come from the deploy profile.

sh

aws s3 ls s3://ledge-api-backups/nightly/ | tail -2

Built to be worked by agents

Ledge ships an MCP server. claude mcp add ledge -- ledge mcp connects Claude Code, and any MCP agent can read, search, create, and edit your notes through it.

Notes are addressed by title, which survives renames, so an agent's references do not go stale.

A terminal opened inside a note knows which note it is in. "Add a TODO section here" needs no explanation.

A prompt code block is a runnable block. ⌘↩ pipes it to the agent and the reply streams in beneath it.

Agents can read your settings and the manual, so "check the Ledge docs" is a fair instruction.

There is no delete tool, and locked notes refuse their bodies to every agent.

Docs: Agents and Ledge

Release 2.5.0

Tag after the migration bake. Checklist in Release runbook. #release

sh

git log --oneline v2.4.1..HEAD | head -3

Done84 ms

9f31c22 storage: chunked uploads for assets over 50 MB
41b0a07 api: rate limit per token, not per IP
c2ade19 fix: retry idempotent writes on 5xx

Lock the notes that matter

Locking encrypts a note's body on disk behind a passphrase. Agents never see it, sync services carry ciphertext, and reading it requires an unlock.

The title, frontmatter, and tags stay visible, so links and navigation keep working.

Search and backlinks skip locked bodies and say how many notes they skipped.

One passphrase covers every locked note. ⌘L relocks, and the vault relocks itself after 15 minutes idle.

Images pasted into a locked note are sealed with it.

A locked note is self-contained. On another machine it unlocks with the passphrase alone. There is no recovery.

Docs: Note Locking

This note is locked. Its body stays sealed on disk, away from agents and search, until you unlock.

Unlock Notes…

dev@mbp notes % ledge cat "Comp review 2026"

Sync with anything, share with git

Notes are plain files in ordinary folders, so syncing them is syncing a folder: iCloud Drive, Dropbox, git, Syncthing, or whatever you already use. There is no database on the side.

Ledge watches the folder and follows outside changes live, even in an open note.

Push a workspace to a git remote and the people you work with clone it. Each clone attaches as an ordinary workspace, and a pull shows up in the sidebar with nothing to refresh.

One note changed in two clones is a git conflict like any other. If a pull rewrites a note you have open, your version keeps the file and the other goes to the workspace trash.

A Sync note in the workspace pulls, commits, and pushes with one ⌘↩.

Profiles never enter the folder, locked notes travel as ciphertext, and the trash stays out of git.

Docs: Keep Notes Synced

Sync

This workspace is a repo. One run commits and pushes every note in it.

sh

git add -A && git commit -m "notes $(date +%F)" || true
git pull --rebase && git push

Ways to use Ledge

Six kinds of notes, each with the manual page that covers it.

Data exploration

sql

select plan, count(*)
from signups group by plan;

Done41 ms

plan | count
------+-------
free | 1204
pro | 187

python

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("signups.csv")
print(df["source"].mode()[0])

Docs: Running Code

Project runbook

cwd: ~/Projects/api

envFile: .env

sh

docker compose up -d db
make migrate

Done3.8 s

✔ Container api-db-1 Started
migrated to 0043_signup_source

Docs: Run a Project from a Note

Incident response

redis

INFO keyspace

Done12 ms

# Keyspace
db0:keys=4812339,expires=0,avg_ttl=0

Docs: Profiles and Secrets

Learning to code

ruby

%w[a b c].each_with_index do |s, i|
puts "#{i}: #{s}"
end

Docs: Running Code

Homelab

sh

zpool list -o name,cap,health

Done1.1 shomelab

NAME CAP HEALTH
tank 81% ONLINE

Docs: Run Code on Remote Hosts

Daily journal

prompt

List the open tasks in [[2026-07-30]]

Done4.2 s

- Send the lease renewal back
- Finish the chapter 4 notes

Docs: Daily Notes and Templates

The notes app underneath

Everything else you expect from a notes app is here.

Your languages

Python, Node, Ruby, and PHP run out of the box. A redis block feeds redis-cli, pointed at staging or prod by the note's REDIS_URL. TypeScript uses the Bun runtime bundled with the app, so ts blocks run with nothing installed. Adding an interpreter is one line in Settings.

"sql": "psql \"$DATABASE_URL\" -f"

Daily notes and templates

⌘J opens today's note, stamped from your daily template. Templates are ordinary notes with {{date}} and {{yesterday}} tokens, and one carrying a prompt block gives every morning a one-keystroke briefing.

promptSummarize [[{{yesterday}}]]

A workspace is a folder

Attach a project folder and its Markdown files become notes where they are, running their blocks in the project. ⌘1 to ⌘9 switch workspaces, and each keeps its own pane layout. Removing an attached folder from Ledge touches no files.

Attach Folder as Workspace…

Live preview

Syntax hides away from the caret: **bold** shows bold, links show their label, tables and images render in place, and a checkbox is clickable. Move the caret in and the exact characters come back. One setting shows every character all the time.

"editor.livePreview": false

Paste anything

Copy part of a web page, a Slack thread, or a Google Doc, and ⌘V pastes it as Markdown: headings, lists, checkboxes, links, and tables included. ⇧⌘V pastes the plain text. An image on the pasteboard lands in the workspace as a file, rendering in place; pasted into a locked note, it is encrypted from the first byte.

![](.ledge-assets/pasted-2026-07-31.png)

Find your way back

⌘P opens a note by title; type # for full-text search. Wikilinks address titles, so a retitle never leaves a stale link. Backlinks and outline each get a panel.

[[Oncall handbook#Paging]]

Tags and favorites

Tag a note with inline #hashtags or a frontmatter tags: line, and ⌥⌘T lists every tag with its count. Press f on a note's row, or click its star, and it sits in a Favorites section at the top of the sidebar, however deep in a folder it lives. Both are frontmatter, so they travel with the file.

favorite: true

Deleting is undoable

A Markdown notebook for developers and DevOps who keep commands in their notes. Write a note, press ⌘↩ on a code block, and its output streams in beneath it. In your shell, in your project, on your machine, or on a server.

Each note has its own shell
Shell blocks run in a persistent shell that belongs to the note. A cd, an exported variable, or an activated virtualenv carries into the next run.
⌘↩ runs the block under the caret. Output streams in beneath it.
⇧⌘↩ sends the block to the note's terminal drawer, a second shell you can keep typing in.
A running block takes input. Answer a sudo password or a [y/N] in the output panel.
cwd: and env: in the frontmatter set where the note's shells start and what they carry.
norun on a fence takes the Run button away. Use it for a command you are quoting, not running.

Point Ledge at a machine over ssh and the notes live there. The server holds the files and runs the shells. The app on your computer is the window onto it.
No account, no service, and no port to open. The only thing between you and the server is ssh.
Shells and running blocks belong to the server. Close the laptop and they keep going. The output is waiting when you open it again.
Your computer, your phone, and a second window can all be on one server at once, each with its own tabs.
Sign in with an ssh key, or with a password kept in the system keychain. Ledge pins the server's host key and refuses any other.

Read, edit, and create notes with live preview. Search, tags, backlinks, daily notes, and wikilinks all work.

items.author: viraj_shah

items.text:
Summary: Three people died at Burning Man in 2026. This was about a quarter of what the crude national rate would predict (~12 deaths). Calculating the age-standardized death rate, we’d expect to see an average of 4.9 deaths. At this rate, seeing 3 deaths is not abnormal. However, Burning Man’s near zero death rate over its existence is abnormal, and likely due to selection bias of healthier attendees and other confounding demographic factors.

The Burning Man event this year (2026) had three confirmed deaths. It made a few headlines as this was the highest recorded number. For an event that has mostly seen no deaths during its 3+ decade existence, this was abnormally high. But I’m curious, compared to the rates we see in the general population, was observing three deaths abnormal? Let’s dive into the numbers and find out for ourselves.

The Black Rock City Census 2025 Population Report has a great demographic breakdown of the 2025 Burning Man population. Of course, we’re comparing 2026 deaths with 2025 data, but we’ll go ahead and say that the attendee makeup is about the same between both years.

Here are some of the standout data points:

Over 70% are returning attendees

75% are ethnically white

80% had a bachelor’s degree or more

The two largest income groups continued to increase in participation, with the second largest income group ($100,000 to $299,999 yearly) representing over a third of attendees.

These slices of Burning Man attendees represent a unique population, not indicative of your average US population. I took the Burning Man age distribution and overlaid that with that of the general US population:

The Burning Man population is significantly younger than the oldest in the US population, where death rates are much higher. Keep this chart in mind going forward.

Let’s do the simplest comparison we can. The crude all-cause mortality rate in the general US population was 909.3 deaths per 100,000 people, per year. And at Burning Man, we observed 3 deaths per approximately 70,000 people in 1 week.

If we scale 909.3 deaths over 100,000 person-years to 70,000 people-weeks (70,000 people * 1 week), we get 12.2 deaths. That is, if we randomly select 70,000 people from the US population and observe them for 1 week, we’d expect to see 12.2 deaths on average.

Before, 3 deaths seemed abnormally high, but now we’re saying that 12.2 deaths, over 4x what we observed, is expected. What gives?

You’ll recall that the Burning Man population is quite unique. The attendees are younger, more educated, and higher earners than the general US population. That might explain why we see such a big difference in expected vs observed rates.

In an ideal world, we would account for age, income, sex, race, education, and all other demographic factors. We would find a reference population that looks as close to the Burning Man population, calculate how many deaths we’d expect to see, and compare that to what we observed at the event.

Let’s look at how some of these factors affect mortality rates.

By race and sex, certain races have a higher death rate. Men also seem to die at a higher rate.

Higher educated people had lower death rates.

And the death rates go up exponentially, the older you are.

Given this, we can find a better estimate for the death rate that accounts for these factors. That process is called standardization. Instead of applying one single number like 909.3 deaths per 100,000 person-years, we can break it down.

To standardize by age, we can use the age specific death rates above. We apply each specific death rate (e.g., 4264 deaths for the 75-84 age group in the chart above) to the number of Burning Man attendees within that age bracket. Doing so, we’d estimate observing 4.9 deaths on average.

Before, we had estimated we should see 12.2 deaths at a Burning Man event, if we were to randomly sample the US population. Now we’re saying 4.9. The big difference between these estimates is that we accounted for age. The Burning Man population skews younger where death rates are lower.

But why did we only look at age? We just saw income, race, sex, etc. has an effect on the death rate. The short answer is, it’s hard, if not impossible to get distributions of the population combining all these variables. We looked at age specifically because it has a huge effect size. Look at the scales in charts above. The age specific death rates are the only ones on a log scale, where the difference between different brackets is well over 10x. Including other factors like race, gender, etc. would be more accurate, but it’s unlikely our estimate would move much from our calculated 4.9 deaths. Plus, our goal is not to keep modifying our method so that our calculations fit what we observed.

We can now ask, how abnormal is observing 3 deaths at Burning Man, given our (age-standardized) estimated death rate of 4.9? To model this, we use a Poisson distribution. It gives us the probability of seeing a given number of deaths in a specific amount of people-time (70,000 people-weeks) at the average death rate we calculated.

There is a 27% chance that we would observe 3 deaths or less, given an average rate of 4.9 deaths. This is also known as a p-value. Why isn’t our p-value greater? Seems like 27% is quite low. By scientific standards, this isn’t abnormal at all. Observing 3 deaths is completely within reason.

However, the relative uncertainty of our point data is quite large at about 58% (1/sqrt(3)). This is the size of the error. If we were talking about death rates in the thousands, we might have an error of 3% or less. But the reality is that at such low counts, our data is considered quite “fuzzy”.

The p-value is even lower if we use the average of all deaths in Burning Man’s existence, which is near zero, instead of our single data point of 3 deaths this year. That is, it is indeed abnormal to observe near 0 deaths every year, given our calculated death rate of 4.9.

You might wonder if further standardizing for race, income, sex, etc. would keep pushing our estimate down toward what we actually observe. It’s plausible it would move it a bit further, but not by much. Age is doing nearly all of the work already, and the other factors have far smaller effect sizes. The more likely explanation for the remaining gap is something no demographic slicing can capture. Burning Man selects for healthier people who are willing and able to spend a week in the desert heat, regardless of their age, race, or income bracket.

Including other factors like race, gender, etc. would be more accurate, but it’s unlikely our estimate would move much from our calculated 4.9 deaths. Plus, our goal is not to keep modifying our method so that our calculations fit what we observed.

We can now ask, how abnormal is observing 3 deaths at Burning Man, given our (age-standardized) estimated death rate of 4.9? To model this, we use a Poisson distribution. It gives us the probability of seeing a given number of deaths in a specific amount of people-time (70,000 people-weeks) at the average death rate we calculated.

There is a 27% chance that we would observe 3 deaths or less, given an average rate of 4.9 deaths. This is also known as a p-value. Why isn’t our p-value greater? Seems like 27% is quite low. By scientific standards, this isn’t abnormal at all. Observing 3 deaths is completely within reason.

However, the relative uncertainty of our point data is quite large at about 58% (1/sqrt(3)). This is the size of the error. If we were talking about death rates in the thousands, we might have an error of 3% or less. But the reality is that at such low counts, our data is considered quite “fuzzy”.

The p-value is even lower if we use the average of all deaths in Burning Man’s existence, which is near zero, instead of our single data point of 3 deaths this year. That is, it is indeed abnormal to observe near 0 deaths every year, given our calculated death rate of 4.9.

You might wonder if further standardizing for race, income, sex, etc. would keep pushing our estimate down toward what we actually observe. It’s plausible it would move it a bit further, but not by much. Age is doing nearly all of the work already, and the other factors have far smaller effect sizes. The more likely explanation for the remaining gap is something no demographic slicing can capture. Burning Man selects for healthier people who are willing and able to spend a week in the desert heat, regardless of their age, race, or income bracket.

items.text:
Introduction

Halfspace is an experimental IDE for
solid modeling with distance fields.

Try the demo

(The demo is best experienced on a computer; mobile Safari has some WebGPU
issues, and pan / tilt / zoom interactions are not yet designed for multitouch)

Halfspace is a showcase app for the Fidget kernel, which is used
for rasterization and meshing. Within the GUI, images are rasterized in
real(ish)-time; models can be exported as either images or triangle meshes:

Since it's 2026, let me note at the outset that this is not vibe-coded.
I've been working on it since
April 2025
and am writing the code using my human brain, for
various reasons
(and Fidget dates back to
2022).

Now, the rest of this writeup assumes some knowledge of implicit surfaces;
please see many previous
writeups for details for more
background info (or just keep reading, you'll be fine).

Why?

I've spent a bunch of time writing implicit kernels, slightly less time writing
GUIs on those kernels, and even less time actually modeling with those tools.

In practice, I don't actually need to do much solid modeling in my daily life,
so most of the stuff that I create is a demo or an example of how to use a
particular kernel.

Still, I've noticed a particular tension when working with implicit surfaces.
Working with low-level implicit surfaces is a bit like writing assembly: it's
low-level, powerful, and annoying. If all you're given is x, y, z
variables – and it's your responsibility to combine them into all the shapes of
your dreams – that can be a painful experience.

When faced with the pain of writing assembly, most people build abstractions on
top of it: high-level languages and libraries that compile down to a low-level
representation. The equivalent here is a standard library of shapes and
transformations: sphere, box, translate, scale, etc.

There's also a less common approach to the pain of assembly: making assembly
itself less painful to write.

My favorite project along those lines is
Kartik Agaram's Mu,
which wraps emulation, tracing, and time-travel debugging around a subset of x86
assembly language.

Halfspace takes both paths. It includes a (small but growing) standard library,
but also makes it easy to build up models incrementally: a complex model can
be split into smaller pieces, which can be parameterized and visualized
individually.

Given that justification, let's unpack the description a bit farther.

Solid modeling

First off, "solid modeling" means that we're focusing on objects with a
definitive inside and outside; you should be able to pick any point in space and
say whether it's inside or outside the model.

This seems obvious, but there's plenty of modeling that doesn't care about that
property: pull up any
video game model viewer
and you'll see plenty of infinitely-thin textured walls, built from a single
fan of triangles.
Since my background is in
CAD/CAM software
(with an emphasis on 3D printing), I want models that can be physically
realized.

There are a bunch of ways to do solid modeling. In most CAD software, a
boundary-representation
geometry kernel
is responsible for stitching a bunch of individual surfaces together into a
solid body. This is a tremendously hard problem – for example, the intersection
of two NURBS
surfaces may not have a closed-form solution!

Dating back to my Master's thesis, I've been working on geometry kernels based
on implicit surfaces. These have the advantage that they can conceivably be
written and fully understood by a single person or small team, so they're a good
fit for personal-scale fabrication software.

This continues in Halfspace: it's a GUI wrapped around the
Fidget geometry kernel. Models can be designed using some
combination of pre-defined primitives and hand-written scripts, and exported as
either images or triangle meshes.

An IDE for distance fields

We could use the Fidget kernel purely at the constructive solid geometry (CSG)
layer, building shapes (spheres, cubes, cylinders, etc) and combining them with
logical operations (union, intersection, difference). Halfspace instead make
the decision to put the underlying distance fields in the foreground.

Let me give you an example of why this matters. Here are two distance fields
for a sawtooth wave, which have the same signs at every point in space, but
different values:

In this visualization, the sign (which defines inside versus outside) is
shown by color (blue versus orange), with the boundary of the shape shown in
white (corresponding to a value of 0). The field values are shown by the
fainter lines, which are spaced at regular intervals (like a topographic map).

Despite having identical signs everywhere, the first field is very poorly behaved.
Look at the vertical edge of the sawtooth: there's a transition from inside
(blue) to outside (orange) without a crossing through zero.

This is a C0 or
"jump" discontinuity,
and it's bad news! Fidget uses automatic differentiation to compute normals, so
the normals across this boundary don't point in the correct direction (compare
the field lines between top and bottom images). In 3D, where we use normals for
shading, this produces incorrect shading in the cabin's shingles:

(If this looks familiar, it's because it's extracted from
an earlier blog post)

Putting distance fields front-and-center makes it easy to diagnose these kind of
issues. In fact, it suggests a further improvement on the sawtooth field: we
can tweak the gradient so that it's 1 everywhere, instead of being bunched up on
the diagonals. Here's a before / after comparison:

Having uniform gradients makes various algorithms better-behaved; Fidget doesn't
require it for correctness, but it may (for example) improve mesh quality.

Halfspace is experimental and cross-platform

Right now, it would be a very bold decision to use Halfspace in any
load-bearing capacity. In the Fidget writeup, here's one of
the project goals:

Finding the "right" APIs for implicit kernels, with the possibility of making
substantial compatibility breaks

Halfspace is similar; it doesn't present APIs to end-users, but I'm flexing my
software architecture skills by building a substantial cross-platform
application, and I'm willing to aggresively iterate and break things as we go.

Speaking of cross-platform, I'm making my life harder by targeting both the web
and native platforms. In the era of supply-chain attacks, being able to share a
web link – instead of asking someone to compile and run your code – is great for
onboarding and casual usage.

To that end, I've been collecting the "Halfspace stack": a set of libraries and
patterns which let me ship a combined native + web application with a minimum of
pain. Right now, here are the core pieces:

Rust for the application (and all dependencies)

egui_dock for the core
window-and-tab abstraction

egui for the GUI

wgpu for both rendering the UI and GPU compute (!)

Rhai for scripting

Speeding up parallel algorithms by distributing work over many workers; this
is a "typical" usage of the library

A thread pool for short-lived background tasks; this is a more unusual
usage, but we can't spawn threads on the web.

Rayon and
wasm-bindgen-rayon,
used for two purposes:

...and a long tail of other libraries and shenanigans

This all deserves a dedicated writeup, and I have complaints about every single
layer of the stack, but overall, it's incredible that everything Just Works™.

Driving Fidget improvements

Another goal of Halfspace is to drive improvements in the Fidget kernel, by
using it in a non-trivial application.

The biggest victory on this front has been ongoing work on
fidget-wgpu. This was
motivated by performance on the web: the native build was pleasantly fast, but
doing rasterization on the CPU was awfully slow ("non-interactive speeds") when
running through a layer of WebAssembly.

After a lot of work on the Fidget side, both rasterization and
post-processing (e.g. shading) can be run purely on the GPU, without any
roundtrips to the CPU.

This was both a performance and architectural win:

We now have native rendering speed on both native and web targets

Fidget implements the canonical rendering logic

Halfspace has thin shaders which draw an RGBA texture

Rendering logic is no longer spread between Fidget (on the CPU) and Halfspace
(with a mix of CPU and GPU code):

(The 2D rendering pipeline is also now fully GPU-accelerated, although it has
slightly fancier shaders in Halfspace, for reasons)

Wrapping up

Halfspace is a thing that exists!

You should try it out, and should probably not use it for critical applications!
If you encounter problems, please file an issue or open a discussion on Github.

Like most of my work, I plan to keep working on it until I have run out of
things to learn from the project.
Also like most of my work, it's
open-source
under the MPLv2 license.

items.title: Doing a Machine Learning PhD While Working in Japan
items.author: pwim
items.summary: I recently completed my PhD in Computer Science at Tokyo Institute of Technology (now the Institute of Science Tokyo) as an American student on the MEXT
items.text:
I recently completed my PhD in Computer Science at Tokyo Institute of Technology (now the Institute of Science Tokyo) as an American student on the MEXT Scholarship. Simultaneously, I continued my work as a software engineer and researcher at Google.

Because it’s relatively rare for an American student to complete their PhD program abroad—as compared to the number of international students that study in America—many people eventually asked me, “But why would you choose Japan?”

This comes with the implication that, given the American tertiary education system’s prestige, I was being foolish by not taking advantage of it. This point of view has merit. American schools do have incredible name recognition worldwide, as well as opportunities that are rare elsewhere. But I chose Japan, and would like to walk you through my experience to give you the pros and cons.

I admittedly did not have a typical background going into my PhD: I had a good fallback since I had already been working at a FAANG, I had meaningful savings, I already had research experience, etc. This made my time in Japan significantly easier and less stressful than for many of my peers. But it was still not a walk in the park.

Doing a PhD is difficult and isolating, which is exacerbated by being an international student in an unfamiliar country. And so, while I overall very much enjoyed my time there and have freely recommended it to many people, the decision to pursue a PhD in Japan should always be considered carefully.

Background

I’m an American and did my undergraduate degree in America, and before Japan, I was a PhD student in Korea. I didn’t complete my doctorate there, but left with a master’s to join Google full time after an internship.

My original research area was automata theory, but at Google I work primarily on on-device language models for keyboards. I have always inhabited an area between pure research and engineering and worked hard to maintain that balance.

I knew that I wanted to finish a PhD eventually, but I had a fairly specific constraint: if possible, I wanted to keep working part time while doing it. I knew there was some precedent for this arrangement at Google, but it was rare.

At the time I started looking seriously at doctorate programs again, I was working from my parents’ house during COVID-19. I had gone from Seoul, to New York for an internship, to Mountain View for a full-time role, and then back to my hometown in the American South. I had enjoyed some of those moves more than others, but the overall effect was that I had a pretty good sense of what I liked and disliked in a place to live. I loved dense cities, I liked being abroad, and I knew that if I was going to do another PhD, I wanted the location itself to be a meaningful part of the experience.

Why I considered Japan

When I started looking into PhD programs again, I was not particularly looking for something in Japan. I was looking for a specific combination of things: a good research fit, a program that did not require me to spend five or more years away from industry, a realistic way to keep working part time, and a place where I would actually want to live.

Japan happened to fit my constraints unusually well. There was a lab in Tokyo doing research that matched my interests, the Japanese PhD system pushes students to graduate in three years, and the visa situation was more flexible than what was available elsewhere.

On top of that, I already knew that I liked dense, walkable megacities from my time in Seoul and New York. Tokyo was the kind of place I could imagine living for several years.

There were also less concrete reasons. Time in Japan is a good conversation starter and door opener. It sets you apart from other applicants and shows that you can take on challenges and do things differently. I do not think this should be your main consideration when choosing a PhD program, but if you are weighing all the options, it is not irrelevant.

Why Japan can be a good place to do a PhD

Overall, Japan has a strong academic culture, especially in STEM due to the University of Tokyo, Kyoto University, Tohoku University, and my alma mater Institute of Science Tokyo. While undoubtedly the most prestigious schools are disproportionately located in North America and Europe, Japan also has some heavy hitters on the world stage. But this can be said about many countries; in Asia specifically, China, Korea, and Singapore each have several top-tier schools.

A flexible student visa

Japan had other qualities that drew me to it. A practical one is that Japan has a relatively lax policy for working while on a student visa.

Japan’s student visa can come with work authorization from day one, provided you file the correct paperwork either in person or online

This work authorization is subject to only mild constraints, like a cap of 28 hours per week during the semester and 8 hours per day during long school breaks, as well as the exclusion of some types of work.

The ability to work part time is an incredible benefit of doing a PhD in Japan that is rare elsewhere. In America, international students can do internships, but not sustained, year-round work. American students can work freely, but it is rare to do more than summer internships and occasional consulting.

Other countries also seem to have strict requirements. For example, in Korea, graduate students on the D-2 visa are only allowed to work part time in limited roles and only after receiving permission from the school and government. Even summer internships in Korea are much more difficult to arrange. While some students I know in Korea would travel back home or to another country for a summer internship, this came at a large cost, to say nothing of the difficulty of traveling long distances. Since computer science and machine learning blend academia and industry so well, and the incentives for joining the industry after graduating are so high, not being able to do industry internships is a major setback for students.

A PhD with a deadline

Another practical point is that, unlike the US and Europe, which often require five or more years to complete a PhD even with a related master’s, the Japanese PhD system pushes you to graduate in three years. The opportunity cost of doing a PhD is high, and the advisor-student relationship can easily become unbalanced. Students often pay the opportunity cost of being out of the workforce for many years, while labs benefit from their research output and are incentivized to keep the student as long as possible, potentially by delaying their graduation. In that context, having a structural time limit is helpful.

However, the downside to this is that three years can feel too short to be able to reach the edge of your field, produce new work, and train as a researcher. In fast-moving fields like machine learning, one can become productive very quickly, but having a shorter PhD time limit pushes students towards less risky and innovative research to mitigate the risk of taking a bet on a research topic, having it fail, and then not having enough time to recover and produce good work before you need to graduate.

A quickly-growing tech scene

A final good reason to do a PhD in Japan, at least in machine learning, is that the tech scene has changed dramatically and offers opportunities to connect with top companies.

When I first looked into moving to Japan, I would not have considered staying in Japan to work at any company other than FAANG. By the time I finished, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, Hugging Face, and Sakana had opened offices in Japan, which made it feel much more viable as a post-PhD destination.

Being already in Japan gives you a leg up in connecting with these companies, and insulates you from a lot of the international competition that you would face in Europe or America.

Why Japan can be a bad place to do a PhD

There are many downsides to doing a PhD: the opportunity cost, increasingly scarce faculty jobs, the publish-or-perish mentality, etc. Likewise, there are downsides to living in Japan: being far from home and loved ones, relatively low pay, social isolation, etc.

On top of this, the combination of doing a PhD in Japan comes with an additional set of challenges that prospective students should be well aware of.

You went to what university?

The first is name recognition. Doing a PhD abroad doesn’t always have to come with a name recognition penalty, but if you travel outside of your immediate geographic area (e.g. outside of America as an American, or Europe as a European), you quickly run into name recognition issues for all but the top, globally-recognized schools.

Many American universities have good name recognition worldwide, but I think you would be harder pressed to find people that could accurately list the best schools in Korea or Japan if they had not lived there—compare this to the generally high name recognition of Cambridge, Oxford, EPFL, or ETH Zurich to non-Europeans.

Imagine you are applying for jobs later and the person doing the initial resume screen has never heard of Tohoku University—which I mention specifically as I think people would assume that “University of Tokyo” was a good school, even if they did not know about it directly, but Tohoku University is less well known outside of Japan, despite it being a phenomenal school. You will likely be passed over in favor of candidates with more familiar credentials, even if they come from lower-caliber schools.

To put this another way: assuming you’ll be a good graduate student either way, my opinion is that the expected outcome of doing a PhD at a good-but-not-top-tier university in your home country is better than doing it at a good-but-not-top-tier university abroad (with the exception of the US, whose mid-tier schools still carry relatively high name recognition worldwide), if your goal is to move back to your home country after graduation.

Of course, name recognition isn’t everything, and doesn’t actually capture how good your university or lab is or how strong of a researcher you are, but when dealing with high variance situations like hiring, having good name recognition eliminates a huge potential downside.

Unnecessary courses

Another downside of the Japanese PhD system is your academic course load. At Tokyo Tech, PhD students were simply unable to take graduate-level technical courses. This is in stark contrast to most other PhD programs I know of, where extremely niche technical courses are available to PhD students, who are able to get consistent, focused face-time with experts in their field that are not from their lab.

On the one hand, this is a good thing. You have three years to finish your PhD and you should spend that time doing research, not taking courses. But in order to graduate, you still have to complete dozens of credits. At my school, these were divided into seminars (effectively free credits just for doing research), humanities, and career development courses.

For the humanities, I was able to take several Japanese courses, which were fun, though not very effective due to the class sizes. However, the career development courses were not useful. Though I am a native English speaker, I was required to take English presentation courses, which were not effective in improving students’ English abilities at all.

I was also required to enroll in several “future career plans” courses that were basically a series of hour-long speeches by alumni. There was very little interaction in these, so even though many of the speakers had interesting backgrounds, it was hard to get any good discussion going. So while this may have served the purpose of introducing potential career paths, it did not allow for any detailed back-and-forth nor did it serve the (presumed) secondary purpose of being a networking event for students.

You published where?

A final issue I saw more of in Japan was the emphasis on domestic journals and conferences for publishing. There is a well-established set of domestic venues for many fields, and students are often encouraged to submit to them. These publications usually appear in Japanese and may have much lighter peer review than major international venues, but they can still count toward graduation requirements, so many students take advantage of them. However, these conferences and journals are not known outside of Japan.

Just being a domestic rather than international venue means that most employers will discount any research published there, since there is no way to easily verify the quality or prestige of the venue. In some cases they can be useful for local networking or practice, but I would be cautious about relying on domestic journals as your main research output if you plan to leave Japan after your PhD.

Where do you want to be after the PhD?

Looking back, I believe the key question to ask yourself before you commit is: where do you want to be after your PhD? The core question about doing one at all, “Is it worth the opportunity cost?” is the same regardless of where you study. Likewise, most questions about whether Japan suits you apply to anyone moving there, not just students. So to me, the decision point comes down to your plans for after your PhD.

If you think you want to stay in Japan after your PhD, the questions you need to ask aren’t unique to being a PhD student, but are the same for nearly everyone who comes to Japan without a set end date:

Are you okay living in a country that’s difficult to fully assimilate into, no matter how long you stay?

Are you okay being far from friends and family?

Are you okay with the pay, and especially with how hard it is to reverse course if you eventually decide you want to move home after all?

If you can’t answer most of these with a confident “Yes,” you should think twice about your future plans.

But, if your plan is to do a PhD in Japan and then leave, your list of questions becomes much shorter. The primary debate is whether you’re willing to risk the loss in name recognition when you return home and compete against peers with household-name credentials. I personally think this is a risk that people do not take seriously enough, especially if you choose a school outside of the top few schools in Japan.

If you are a strong student and do good research, the hope is that your merits should speak for themselves and potential employers will recognize them. But I do not think this is something you should rely on happening, especially in an increasingly competitive and uncertain job market. This potential downside of choosing Japan can be so great that it outweighs all of the good things about Japan, and so it should be considered carefully.

In short, you are stuck with a hard choice: move back home after graduation, or commit fully to Japan. The latter option is attractive in Japan, as evidenced by the number of “lifers” that you will encounter, but it is still risky. You are tying yourself to a culture that is difficult to integrate into, and the longer you stay, the more difficult it becomes to reverse course.

Finding the right lab

The critical first step to getting a PhD, in Japan and elsewhere, is finding a lab and a professor to work with. There should be a research fit (it can be loose, but there should be some meaningful connection) and a personality fit (do you have the same work style, does your professor micromanage when you want hands off, etc.). Each of these greatly narrows down the prospective field of professors.

Add to this that you are restricting yourself to Japan—which admittedly has many good universities to choose from, but it is still just one country—and that the research and personality fit has to go both ways. Suddenly, you have very few options.

Then there’s the fact that Japan is a desirable country to live in for people all over the world, so professors are inundated with prospective student emails. You have to stand out from a crowd of other, presumably highly-qualified, applicants, and they must make sure you are a serious student and not just looking to join their lab in order to be in Japan.

How I did it

Over time, I had identified a few labs that might be a good fit for my research and other criteria. I only considered Tokyo, so this really narrowed things down. I read up on the current students’ research, what the professor was working on, what the trend of the lab was, etc. I was looking for labs with many international students, a hands-off professor, and research similar to my intended area in Japanese, Chinese, and Korean language modeling.

I happened to meet a graduate student from my eventual lab at a conference and had an in-person chat and some follow-up emails with him. I also had a friend that was a graduate student in the same department, though in a different lab. He was able to put me in contact with another graduate student from the lab. I managed to briefly visit the lab on a business trip to Japan before COVID-19, where I arranged to meet with the professor for an informal meeting.

These interactions allowed me to scope out the lab and the professor, establish a rapport, demonstrate that I was serious, and discuss the possibility of being a graduate student there. There was interest on both sides, but I was still early in my career, and I was not ready to leave my job yet.

Later, as I passed the two-year mark at my work, I began to arrange my proposal to switch to part-time work and a full-time PhD. My managers were largely on board and this ended up going pretty smoothly.

I reached back out to the professor to tell him I was applying. We exchanged some more phone calls and held a series of research interviews, which more or less sealed the deal.

Funding the degree: MEXT and the three-year clock

I knew applying for the MEXT Scholarship would be a good next step, both for the prestige and also to help offset some of the costs of moving to and living in Japan.

Few options for financial assistance

The MEXT Scholarship is one of the main funding paths available to international graduate students, and I would not recommend doing your PhD in Japan if you do not have it or something similar. Self-funded PhD students are common in Japan, so universities do not always have robust scholarships available, and you will likely not be paid by your lab—at least, not an amount that would be comfortable to live on.

Working part time can alleviate financial issues, but it is better to have your funding set up unconditionally, rather than adding an additional stressor onto an already stressful PhD. All of this is significantly different from doing a PhD in the US or Europe, so it may come as a surprise to those considering Japan for graduate school.

For some context, the MEXT scholarship generally grants tuition support, airfare to Japan, and, for doctoral students, a monthly stipend of about 145,000 yen (approximately 900 US dollars at the time of writing). This is enough to live on, but not enough to completely remove money as a source of stress, especially if you live alone in Tokyo.

The two flavors of MEXT Scholarship

Embassy Track

Japanese consulates are allocated a few scholarship spots and hold interviews for candidates within their districts. This track is extremely competitive, as consulates are given very few openings. It also technically comes with you foregoing your ability to choose your eventual university and laboratory. In the application, you are allowed to rank several universities and laboratories as your top choices, but you aren’t guaranteed to get placed at any of them.

I took the interview in Atlanta and bombed miserably. In retrospect, I had a weak story for why I wanted to go to Japan. What I said was true: I was interested in Japanese culture, I had found a lab that did what I wanted to do, I had a strong research background and experience living abroad, etc., but it just wasn’t very compelling overall. I think it looked like I was just someone who wanted to take a break from work and live in Japan for a few years, rather than someone who was striving for it.

University Recommendation Track

After the consulate interview results came out, my future advisor suggested I apply for the other MEXT track: the University Recommendation Track. To be honest, I did not know that this existed at the time, and if I had, I would have just done that in the first place.

This track involves first applying to the university of your choice directly, and once you are accepted, asking them to refer you to MEXT. You typically have already come to an agreement with a specific professor to join their lab, and they write in support of you.

I am not sure how many scholarship spots each university is allocated in this program, but my guess is that it is simultaneously harder and easier than the Embassy Track. It is harder in that the bar to apply is much higher, since you must have a professor argue on your behalf; however it is easier in that if you have a professor’s strong support, you are very likely to receive it. This is unlike the Embassy Track where you have significantly less agency over the situation, and it is a good choice if you have a strong research fit with or connection to a professor.

The three-year limit

The MEXT Scholarship only guarantees you funding for a three-year period, with limited opportunities for extension. This strongly couples with the norm of completing a PhD in Japan in three years, and imposes a more tangible deadline on your graduation.

You can usually extend your time as a graduate student by several years just by filling out some forms and talking with your advisor. But, if the money runs out, you are left in a bad situation.

In my particular case, I was a student for six months beyond my MEXT allocation due to bureaucratic issues with my PhD thesis submission, and because I began my PhD by taking a leave of absence for a semester since I was not yet able to enter the country due to COVID-19 (but this time still counted towards my MEXT scholarship). I wasn’t taking any classes or even really required to be at the university at all, but since my MEXT had run out, so too had my tuition waiver. Not only was I no longer getting my MEXT stipend, but I was also on the hook for my tuition fees which, even though they are an order of magnitude less than US tuition, were still non-negligible. I had the money to cover this, but someone who was relying totally on the MEXT scholarship for their finances would have been in a difficult spot.

Working part time during a PhD

Overall, I would recommend trying to work part time while doing a PhD if you are in Japan, but only if you already have a strong research background and some industry experience. You need some time to ramp up your research/engineering skills and saturate your research pipeline so you always have something to work on. If you aren’t already comfortable in these areas, you will end up “half-assing two things instead of whole-assing one thing,” which will be extremely bad for the outcome of your PhD and could burn a bridge with your employer.

My specific situation in Japan was somewhat special. I transferred from being a full-time employee at Google in the US to being a part-time PhD Researcher in the Tokyo Google office working two days per week. I’ve received a lot of queries about how it worked and how one can get a similar role, but overall, this is not a very repeatable situation. It required the Japanese government, my lab, and Google to all be okay with the arrangement, and it helped that my Google team happened to have a subteam in Tokyo that I could immediately transfer to.

Having the government on board by default makes the process much easier, but finding a position is still non-trivial, though my feeling is that (especially smaller) companies are starved for hyper-niche technical talent, so it is a win-win for them to hire someone part time to get access to your skills at a reduced cost.

Often, then, the most difficult aspect is getting your advisor on board. While they cannot actually prevent you from working part time if you want, other than by following through on a threat to kick you out of the lab, your advisor has an immense amount of influence over your immediate future, so you risk a lot by going against them. My advisor, thankfully, was supportive of it, though it would be different if the student started doing poorly in their research. Not all advisors are this way.

Still, I know of many people in Japan who worked part time at interesting startups throughout their entire PhD. This is a very viable path that can greatly boost your quality of life, assuming you can juggle work and research, as well as give you a leg up after you graduate.

At the lab

Despite my lab being fairly international, there was a clear divide between the Japanese and international students. Everyone got along and there were no major issues, but the separation was tangible. This mainly manifested as a divide over who collaborated on projects together, with international students primarily working with international students and Japanese students with Japanese students.

This makes sense in some ways, as the language barrier can be hard to overcome, especially in hyper-technical contexts, but it is not ideal. If there are not many international students in your laboratory and your Japanese skill is not sufficient for technical conversations (like mine), you may find yourself with few immediate collaborators.

As a PhD student, it is important to learn how to network and find people with whom you can conduct good research, but as a beginning PhD student in particular, it is helpful to have a supportive set of labmates who you can work with and learn from.

I ended up becoming pretty good friends with some of my labmates and we would hang out outside of school. This helped a lot to ease the isolation that many people feel in Japan, since labmates are basically primed to be friendly in a way that coworkers are not. Our lab also hosted semesterly dinners, game nights, and other small events to help break the ice.

One stark difference that I noticed in Japan, compared to the US and Korea, was the divide between graduate and undergraduate students—or, perhaps, the divide between a graduate student at a lab, and the rest of the student body.

In the US, I felt there was very little barrier between me and the graduate students in my department. I saw them in passing and knew some by name. They taught my classes, hosted and attended seminars, etc. In Korea, there was a greater divide, but I still interacted with undergraduates often through seminars, courses, general events, and students joining our lab.

However, in Japan, I felt that graduate students and undergraduates were essentially two different species that did not interact. I struggle to think of a single time I talked with an undergraduate student who was not part of my lab. There were no opportunities to be a teaching assistant (which some people dread, but I was looking forward to) and no random hallways in which to bump into people.

Even interacting with other graduate students outside of my immediate sphere was difficult, as my lab was behind two key-access doors on top of a random building on campus. This was quite different from in the US and Korea, where the lab space, classroom space, and general departmental student body space were all well integrated.

I found this a bit of a bummer. Of course, by the time I was a graduate student in Japan, I was nearing 30, and so probably would not have made many friends with the much younger general student population. Still, it made my time at Tokyo Tech feel more like rote work and less like being in a thriving academic community.

Overall, while my lab experience was very nice, the university itself offered little else in terms of socializing. You cannot rely on the crutch of being in school to build a social network the way you might as an undergraduate, so you have to be proactive about cultivating relationships outside of the university.

Living in Tokyo

My daily life in Tokyo was quite different from my experience in big American cities, but similar to Seoul.

Making friends

Being an international student in these countries means you are, de facto, an outsider. A common sentiment among foreigners in Japan is that even if you speak perfect Japanese, have a Japanese partner, work in a Japanese company, adhere perfectly to Japanese customs, etc., you will never fully fit in. I don’t speak perfect Japanese, nor do I have a Japanese partner or employment in a Japanese company or a perfect grasp of Japanese culture, and I very clearly felt the gap while living there.

The Japanese friends I made were all either from my lab, or native Japanese people that had lived abroad. Overall, my friend group was dominated by expats. Many people may interpret this as defeating the purpose of living in Tokyo and fully immersing in Japanese culture, but it is nearly a fact of life. As I explained above, you should not expect to make a huge group of Japanese student friends at your university as a graduate student. Fortunately, the expat scene in Tokyo is large and diverse, at least relative to Seoul in my experience.

I tried a few different ways to meet new friends, like attending tech meetups or even Bumble BFF, but in the end I met my closest friends during chance encounters at coffee shops or on the street. Even in my home country, encounters like this are difficult to come by. In Japan, especially if you are in Tokyo, the situation is even worse, since the likelihood of meeting a foreigner that is not a short-term visitor is very low and making Japanese friends is difficult.

All this is to say, if you don’t already have a support group in Japan, you must work very hard to deliberately build your friend group.
